document.title: Archer K. Blood Oral History Excerpt
document.authors: Archer K. Blood, ADST Foreign Affairs Oral History Project (interview by Henry Precht)
document.publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Soviet Invasion of Afghanistan, 1979: Not Trump’s Terrorists, Nor Zbig’s Warm Water Ports | National Security Archive
document.note: Blood describes the situation in Afghanistan and how he came to substitute for Amstutz. He explains, via the Indians, why the Afghans would never approve his return to Kabul as head of mission because of his "secret meetings with Amin." Also recalls his 1971 Dhaka dissent cable.

persons.role: US diplomat in New Delhi who took over the US Embassy in Kabul as acting chargé for about six weeks in late 1979; the interviewee

I think I was the last Westerner to see Amin alive

events.description: US Ambassador Adolph 'Spike' Dubs shot in Kabul; Afghan and Soviet roles seen as equivocal.
Archer Blood sent from New Delhi to run the US Embassy in Kabul for about six weeks while Amstutz took a break.
Blood met Hafizullah Amin and told him no resumption of aid until the US was satisfied about the Afghan role in Dubs's death.
Soviet invasion of Afghanistan at Christmas 1979; Amin killed by the Soviets.
Blood met Monty Diction in Sri Lanka and learned the Afghans said he had held secret meetings with Amin.
Ambassador Adolph Dubs was shot/murdered in Kabul.
Blood sent from New Delhi to take over the Kabul embassy for about six weeks after Amstutz wanted a break.
Blood called on Foreign Minister Shah Mohammed Dost and learned Rolanfahadi was not dead.
Blood met Hafizullah Amin to convey that US aid would not resume until the Afghans addressed Dubs's death.
Soviets invaded Afghanistan at Christmas and killed Amin.
Blood stopped in Sri Lanka and spoke with Monty Diction about why the Afghans rejected him as chargé.

sources_cited: ADST Foreign Affairs Oral History Project interview of Archer K. Blood by Henry Precht, 27 June 1989
key_claims: Blood believes he was the last Westerner to see Hafizullah Amin alive before the Soviets killed him in the December 1979 invasion.
Washington's message to Amin was that US aid would not resume until the Afghan role in Ambassador Dubs's death was explained; the Afghan and Soviet roles were described as equivocal.
The Soviets were building up in Afghanistan incrementally before the invasion, with US estimates of 8,000-12,000 personnel, mostly military advisers.
Blood was surprised by the invasion because the Afghan government was not close to military defeat and the Soviets could have continued infiltrating troops.
Blood thinks the only plausible reason for the invasion was the Soviet need to remove Amin.
Afghanistan rejected Blood as chargé; he suspects the cause was US New Delhi press briefings that publicized resistance successes, or contacts with anti-regime Afghans.
The Afghans reportedly claimed Blood had secret meetings with Amin, which he denies.
